name: A. de Cabezón
bio: Spanish Renaissance composer and organist, blind from childhood, who served as court musician to Isabella of Portugal and later Philip II, traveling with the royal court through Italy, the Netherlands, and England. His tientos and diferencias (keyboard variation sets) mark him as the first major Iberian keyboard composer and one of the most important composers of his time.

name: W. Byrd
bio: English Renaissance composer and organist, a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal who wrote Latin sacred vocal music and consort works. His keyboard works appear in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book and My Ladye Nevells Booke.

name: J.P. Sweelinck
bio: Dutch composer, organist, and pedagogue whose work straddled the end of the Renaissance and represented a pinnacle in keyboard contrapuntal complexity and refinement before J.S. Bach. He wrote toccatas, and his teaching of pupils such as Scheidt and Scheidemann helped establish the north German organ tradition.

name: J. Bull
bio: English keyboard virtuoso and composer, some of whose works were collected in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book. He spent his final years in the Spanish Netherlands as organist of Antwerp Cathedral.

name: G. Frescobaldi
bio: Italian virtuoso keyboard player and composer who served as organist of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. His toccatas, canzonas, and ricercars for organ and harpsichord influenced later composers, including J.S. Bach.

name: O. Gibbons
bio: English composer and keyboard player, a contributor to Parthenia, the first printed collection of English virginal music. Organist of Westminster Abbey and the Chapel Royal, he was admired as the finest keyboard performer of his generation.

name: J.J. Froberger
bio: German composer and organist. A student of Frescobaldi, he helped standardize the keyboard suite form.

name: L. Couperin
bio: French composer, organist, and harpsichordist who was the first major member of the Couperin musical dynasty. He invented the unmeasured prelude for harpsichord and was the first Couperin to serve as organist at Saint-Gervais in Paris.

name: J.C. Kerll
bio: German organist and composer who wrote keyboard toccatas and canzonas. He was Kapellmeister at the Munich court and later a court organist in Vienna, and an organ improvisation on a subject given by the sovereign became so famous that Mattheson recalled it in 1740.

name: J. d'Anglebert
bio: French harpsichordist and composer who succeeded Chambonnieres as harpsichordist to Louis XIV. His 1689 collection of harpsichord suites, Pieces de clavecin, includes a table of ornaments, the most sophisticated before Couperin's.

name: D. Buxtehude
bio: Danish-German organist and composer, a central figure of North German organ music who brought it to its high point. He was organist at the Marienkirche in Lübeck, and Bach walked 250 miles to hear him play.

name: B. Pasquini
bio: Italian composer and renowned virtuoso keyboard player, one of the most important Italian composers for harpsichord between Frescobaldi and Domenico Scarlatti. He was organist at Santa Maria in Vallicella from 1657, then at Santa Maria Maggiore and Santa Maria in Aracoeli in Rome from 1664, and left a large body of keyboard music, mostly preserved in manuscript.

name: J. Krieger
bio: German composer and organist who directed church music in Zittau for over half a century. Handel studied his Anmuthige Clavier-Übung and took a copy to England.

name: J. Pachelbel
bio: German composer and organist who brought the south German organ school to its peak. Beyond the famous Canon in D, his keyboard works include the Hexachordum Apollinis variations and numerous chorale preludes and toccatas for organ.

name: J.C.F. Fischer
bio: German Baroque composer whose Ariadne Musica features preludes and fugues. He was among the first to apply orchestral suite principles to the harpsichord.

name: G. Torelli
bio: Italian violinist and composer of the Bolognese school. His Op. 8 concertos include the Christmas Concerto.

name: H. Purcell
bio: English Baroque composer and harpsichordist, generally considered one of the greatest English composers. Organist of Westminster Abbey from 1679 and later court harpsichordist to James II, he left only a small body of keyboard music, chiefly harpsichord suites and organ pieces.

name: J. Kuhnau
bio: German composer and organist at the Thomaskirche in Leipzig, where he was J.S. Bach's immediate predecessor as Cantor. His Biblical Sonatas (1700) are pioneering examples of programmatic keyboard music.

name: A. Scarlatti
bio: Italian Baroque composer who was the father of Domenico Scarlatti and a leading figure in Neapolitan opera. Though best known for vocal music, his keyboard toccatas and variations contributed to the Italian harpsichord tradition.

name: G. Bohm
bio: German Baroque organist and composer who served as organist at the Johanniskirche in Lüneburg. He is notable for his development of the chorale partita and for his influence on the young J.S. Bach.

name: E. Jacquet de la Guerre
bio: French harpsichordist and composer. Her Premier livre de pieces de clavessin (1687) was one of only a handful of harpsichord collections published in 17th-century France.

name: F. Couperin
bio: French Baroque composer and harpsichordist known as "le Grand," who published four books of harpsichord ordres (suites). His treatise L'Art de toucher le clavecin (1716) covers keyboard technique and ornamentation.

name: L. Marchand
bio: French organist, harpsichordist, and composer, one of the best-known French virtuosos of his time. According to later German accounts, he left Dresden in 1717 rather than face a planned keyboard contest with J.S. Bach, a story found in no French documents and generally doubted.

name: G.P. Telemann
bio: Prolific German Baroque composer who was the most famous musician in Germany during his lifetime. His keyboard output includes fantasias, fugues, and chorale preludes.

name: J.-P. Rameau
bio: French composer and music theorist who was the leading French harpsichord composer alongside Couperin. He wrote three books of harpsichord pieces, and his Treatise on Harmony (1722) transformed music theory.

name: J.G. Walther
bio: German organist, composer, and lexicographer, a friend and cousin of J.S. Bach. He composed organ chorale preludes and published the Musicalisches Lexicon (1732), the first German music dictionary.

name: J.S. Bach
bio: German composer and virtuoso organist of the late Baroque, widely regarded as one of the greatest composers in Western musical history. His works include the Well-Tempered Clavier, Goldberg Variations, and organ works.

name: G.F. Handel
bio: German-British Baroque composer celebrated for his operas, oratorios, and concerti grossi. He published his eight suites for harpsichord in 1720, and his organ concertos were conceived to showcase him as a virtuoso composer-performer.

name: D. Scarlatti
bio: Italian composer who spent much of his life in the service of the Portuguese and Spanish royal families. He is best known for his 555 keyboard sonatas.

name: D. Zipoli
bio: Italian Baroque composer and organist who became a Jesuit missionary in South America. His Sonate d'intavolatura per organo e cimbalo was published in 1716, and his music soon spread across South America, from Paraguay to Bolivia and Peru.

name: B. Galuppi
bio: Italian composer and virtuoso harpsichordist nicknamed "Il Buranello" who was highly regarded for his keyboard sonatas. He served as maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice and gave weekly harpsichord recitals at the Russian imperial court.

name: W.F. Bach
bio: German composer and organist, the eldest son of J.S. Bach, who supervised his musical education closely. He remained a renowned organist throughout his life and was renowned for his improvisatory skills.

name: C.P.E. Bach
bio: German composer and keyboardist, the fifth child of J.S. Bach. His Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments was called "the school of schools" by Haydn, and Mozart declared him "the father."

name: P. Nardini
bio: Italian violinist and composer who studied with Giuseppe Tartini, served at the court of the Duke of Württemberg in Stuttgart, and from 1770 was music director at the court in Florence until his death. He was known for the singing, expressive quality of his playing and wrote violin concertos and sonatas.

name: A. Soler
bio: Spanish composer and organist at the monastery of El Escorial. He composed around 150 keyboard sonatas, many believed to have been written for the Infante Don Gabriel, which are comparable to those of Domenico Scarlatti.

name: J. Haydn
bio: Austrian composer and central figure of the Classical period known as the "Father of the Symphony." He composed numerous piano trios.

name: J.C. Bach
bio: German-born Classical composer, the youngest son of J.S. Bach. His Op. 5 sonatas were among the first published for pianoforte, and his music strongly influenced the young Mozart.

name: J. Schobert
bio: German harpsichordist and composer active in Paris who influenced the young Mozart. He died with most of his family after eating poisonous mushrooms.

name: M. L. Sirmen
bio: Italian violinist and composer who trained at the Ospedale dei Mendicanti in Venice and studied with Tartini. She toured Europe with her husband and published string quartets and violin concertos.

name: D. Cimarosa
bio: Italian Classical composer best known for comic operas, who was also a capable keyboard player. His 88 keyboard sonatas were written for harpsichord or early piano.

name: B. Campagnoli
bio: Italian violinist and composer who studied with Nardini and led the Gewandhaus orchestra in Leipzig. He wrote Caprices for solo viola and a violin method.

name: M. Clementi
bio: Italian-born British pianist and composer called "the father of the pianoforte" for his pioneering development of piano technique. He also wrote the etude collection Gradus ad Parnassum.

name: W.A. Mozart
bio: Composer and keyboard prodigy widely regarded as one of the greatest in Western music. He wrote 27 piano concertos and 18 piano sonatas and helped establish the piano concerto as a major genre.

name: M.T. von Paradis
bio: Austrian pianist, singer, and composer who lost her sight in early childhood. Mozart may have composed his Piano Concerto No. 18 for her, and she later founded a music school for young women in Vienna.

name: J.L. Dussek
bio: Czech pianist and composer who was one of the first piano virtuosos to travel widely throughout Europe and one of the first to place the piano sideways on stage.

name: H. de Montgeroult
bio: French composer and pianist, recognized as one of the finest fortepiano performers and improvisers of her time. In 1795 she became a first-class piano professor at the Paris Conservatoire, teaching the men's class and the only woman given that rank in that period, before resigning in 1798; her published piano course contains 114 études.

name: D. Steibelt
bio: German pianist and composer who was a prominent keyboard virtuoso in Paris and London before settling in Saint Petersburg. He is reported to have challenged Beethoven to a trial of skill.

name: L. van Beethoven
bio: German composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras. Despite progressive hearing loss, he produced masterworks including 32 piano sonatas.

name: J.B. Cramer
bio: German-born English pianist, composer, and music publisher who was one of the leading piano virtuosos of his generation. His 84 Etudes for piano remain widely used in piano pedagogy.

name: J.N. Hummel
bio: Austrian composer and piano virtuoso who studied with Mozart and Clementi. His piano works bridged Classical and Romantic styles, and his treatise on piano playing remained a standard text for many years.

name: J. Field
bio: Irish pianist and composer credited with originating the piano nocturne as a lyrical character piece. His lyrical piano style and 18 nocturnes influenced Chopin, Mendelssohn, Liszt, and other Romantic composers.

name: C.M. von Weber
bio: German composer, conductor, and virtuoso pianist, a crucial figure in the development of German Romantic opera. His Konzertstück in F minor inspired Chopin, Liszt, and Mendelssohn, and his Invitation to the Dance is an early example of the Romantic concert waltz.

name: M. Szymanowska
bio: Polish pianist and composer admired by Goethe, who addressed a poem to her. She had a salon in St. Petersburg, and she composed etudes, nocturnes, and mazurkas.

name: C. Czerny
bio: Austrian pianist, composer, and teacher who studied under Beethoven and taught Franz Liszt. He is best remembered for his extensive collection of piano exercises and etudes that remain staples of piano pedagogy.

name: J.V. Voříšek
bio: Bohemian composer and pianist active in Vienna, where he met Beethoven in 1814 and became a close friend of Schubert. His Impromptus, Op. 7 (1822) are among the earliest pieces to carry that title.

name: I. Moscheles
bio: Bohemian-born pianist and composer, a leading figure of European concert life before joining Mendelssohn at the Leipzig Conservatory.

name: F. Schubert
bio: Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras whose works include piano sonatas, impromptus, and Moments Musicaux.

name: C. de Bériot
bio: Belgian violinist and composer who founded the Franco-Belgian school of violin playing. He wrote ten violin concertos, taught at the Brussels Conservatoire, and was the husband of the mezzo-soprano Maria Malibran.

name: L. Farrenc
bio: French composer, pianist, and pedagogue who held the piano professorship at the Paris Conservatoire for three decades. She composed three symphonies and a Nonet for winds and strings, and in 1850 won equal pay with her male colleagues.

name: Fanny Mendelssohn
bio: German composer and pianist of the early Romantic era, and the elder sister of Felix Mendelssohn. A prolific talent, she wrote over 460 works spanning songs, piano pieces, and chamber music, some of which appeared under her brother's name during her lifetime.

name: F. Mendelssohn
bio: German composer, pianist, and conductor of the early Romantic period. His Songs Without Words are piano miniatures, and he was a champion of J.S. Bach's music.

name: F. Chopin
bio: Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic period who wrote primarily for solo piano. His technically demanding and poetically expressive works include nocturnes, etudes, and ballades.

name: R. Schumann
bio: German composer and influential music critic of the Romantic era. His piano works include Carnaval and Kinderszenen.

name: F. Liszt
bio: Hungarian composer and the foremost piano virtuoso of his time. He is credited as the first pianist to give solo recitals in the modern sense, pushed the boundaries of technique and harmonic language, and influenced generations of pianists as a teacher.

name: S. Thalberg
bio: Swiss-Austrian pianist and composer who rivaled Liszt. He developed the "three-hand" technique, placing melodies in the thumb while surrounding them with cascading arpeggios.

name: C.-V. Alkan
bio: French virtuoso pianist and composer whose piano works are among the most technically demanding in the repertoire. He adopted a reclusive life from 1848, and his music has been steadily revived since the 1960s.

name: S. Heller
bio: Hungarian pianist and composer who settled in Paris, where he became closely acquainted with Chopin, Berlioz and Liszt and was favorably judged by Schumann. His etudes remain popular with music teachers and students.

name: A. von Henselt
bio: German virtuoso pianist and composer who settled in Russia and strongly influenced the Russian school of pianism. Rachmaninoff considered his etudes equal to the better-known studies of Chopin and Liszt.

name: C. Schumann
bio: German pianist and composer who was one of the most distinguished concert pianists of the Romantic era. A child prodigy, she concertized for over 60 years and championed the works of her husband Robert and of Brahms.

name: C. Franck
bio: Belgian-French composer, pianist, and organist who wrote the Prelude, Chorale and Fugue for piano solo (1884) and the Symphonic Variations for piano and orchestra. He became professor at the Paris Conservatoire in 1872.

name: É. Lalo
bio: French composer of Spanish descent best known for the Symphonie espagnole, a virtuosic showpiece for violin and orchestra. He also wrote the opera Le roi d'Ys and a cello concerto.

name: B. Smetana
bio: Czech composer and pianist regarded in his homeland as the father of Czech music. His piano works include the Czech Dances.

name: L.M. Gottschalk
bio: American pianist and composer who was the first internationally acclaimed American concert pianist. His piano works, blending Creole, Caribbean, and Latin American rhythms with Romantic virtuosity, anticipated ragtime and jazz.

name: A. Rubinstein
bio: Russian pianist, composer, and conductor who founded the Saint Petersburg Conservatory. One of the greatest keyboard virtuosos of the 19th century, his historical recital series surveyed the entire history of piano music.

name: H. von Buelow
bio: German conductor, virtuoso pianist, and student of Liszt who premiered Liszt's Piano Sonata in B minor.

name: T. Leschetizky
bio: Polish pianist and composer. Many pianists studied with him in Vienna, including Schnabel, Friedman, and Paderewski.

name: J. Brahms
bio: German composer and pianist of the mid-Romantic period whose piano works include two concertos, rhapsodies, and intermezzi.

name: C. Saint-Saens
bio: French composer, organist, and pianist who was a child prodigy and prolific creator. He wrote five piano concertos, of which No. 2 is probably the most popular.

name: M. Balakirev
bio: Russian composer and pianist who led The Mighty Handful, the group of nationalist composers. His piano fantasy Islamey was considered the most difficult piano piece of its time.

name: M. Bruch
bio: German Romantic composer whose Violin Concerto No. 1 in G minor is one of the most popular violin concertos in the solo violin repertoire. He also wrote the Scottish Fantasy for violin and orchestra.

name: M. Mussorgsky
bio: Russian composer whose Pictures at an Exhibition is a virtuosic work for solo piano. A member of The Five, he was an innovator who often defied Western conventions and wrote vocal lines that imitate natural speech, inspiring later Russian composers such as Shostakovich and Prokofiev.

name: P.I. Tchaikovsky
bio: Russian composer whose Piano Concerto No. 1 in B-flat minor is one of the most popular concertos in the repertoire. His piano works include The Seasons and the Grand Sonata.

name: A. Dvorak
bio: Czech composer whose piano works include the Slavonic Dances (originally for piano four hands), the Humoresques, and a piano concerto. His music blends Romantic lyricism with Bohemian and Moravian folk elements.

name: C. Tausig
bio: Polish piano virtuoso, famed for flawless technique. He is remembered for his transcriptions and studies, and died at twenty-nine.

name: E. Grieg
bio: Norwegian composer and pianist whose Piano Concerto in A minor is among the most beloved Romantic concertos. He also wrote Lyric Pieces for piano.

name: G. Fauré
bio: French composer whose piano works include nocturnes, barcarolles, and impromptus, and whose music bridged the Romantic and Modern eras. His subtle harmonic language, with its unresolved mild discords and colouristic effects, anticipated Impressionism; Ravel was among his pupils.

name: T. Carreño
bio: Venezuelan pianist, composer, and conductor nicknamed the "Valkyrie of the Piano". A child prodigy who performed for Abraham Lincoln at the White House, she toured internationally for decades as a leading concert pianist and composed about 75 works, including piano pieces, works for voice and piano, and choral hymns such as the Himno a Bolívar, performed in Caracas in 1885.

name: L. Janáček
bio: Czech composer whose piano cycles include On an Overgrown Path, whose first volume is built on Moravian folk melodies, and In the Mists. His Piano Sonata 1.X.1905, written in memory of a worker killed in a 1905 Brno demonstration, survives through a copy owned by the pianist Ludmila Tučková, after he burned one movement and threw the other two into the Vltava.

name: M. Moszkowski
bio: Polish-German pianist, composer and teacher best known for his Spanish Dances, Op. 12, which brought him much popularity and the enthusiasm of admirers throughout Europe. He moved to Paris in 1897.

name: A. Lyadov
bio: Russian composer and teacher associated with the nationalist Belyayev circle in Saint Petersburg. He composed many piano miniatures, including preludes, mazurkas, and the Musical Snuffbox, as well as the orchestral tone poems Baba-Yaga and The Enchanted Lake.

name: C. Chaminade
bio: French composer and pianist whose works include the popular Flute Concertino. She toured widely as a pianist performing her own works and became the first woman composer awarded the Légion d'honneur.

name: E. Elgar
bio: English composer, largely self-taught, whose Enigma Variations (1899) established him as the leading British composer of his generation. A working violinist and violin teacher in Worcester long before that success, he wrote the Violin Concerto in B minor (1910) for Fritz Kreisler and the Violin Sonata in E minor (1918).

name: I. Albeniz
bio: Spanish pianist and composer whose masterwork Iberia is one of the most challenging suites in the piano literature. A child prodigy who first performed in public at age four, he began touring northern Spain at nine with his father and sister.

name: I.J. Paderewski
bio: Polish pianist, composer, and statesman. He served as Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Poland in 1919 and signed the Treaty of Versailles.

name: E. MacDowell
bio: American composer and pianist who was one of the first American composers to win international recognition. His Woodland Sketches include To a Wild Rose, and he composed two piano concertos.

name: C. Debussy
bio: French composer who was a leading figure of Impressionist music, though he rejected the term. His piano works include Clair de Lune and the Preludes, and he developed his own style of harmony and orchestral colouring.

name: E. Nazareth
bio: Brazilian pianist and composer, especially noted for his maxixe and choro compositions and for the works he called 'Brazilian tangos'. He also composed waltzes and polkas, and made a major contribution to the development of Brazil's national music style.

name: A. Glazunov
bio: Russian composer, conductor, and long-serving director of the St Petersburg Conservatory. His Violin Concerto in A minor dates from 1904.

name: J. Sibelius
bio: Finnish composer of the late Romantic and early modern periods, celebrated for his tone poem Finlandia. He composed seven symphonies and the Violin Concerto in D minor (1904, revised 1905).

name: F. Busoni
bio: Pianist, composer, and theorist who was among the greatest piano virtuosos of his generation. He made transcriptions of Bach and wrote a monumental Piano Concerto.

name: E. Satie
bio: French composer and pianist whose simple piano pieces, such as the Gymnopédies and Gnossiennes, helped steer French music toward a leaner style. He influenced Ravel and Debussy, and some writers see him as an influence on minimalism and on later composers such as John Cage.

name: A. Beach
bio: American composer and pianist who was the first successful American female composer of large-scale art music. A child prodigy, she concertized extensively.

name: E. Granados
bio: Spanish pianist and composer whose Goyescas was inspired by the paintings of Goya.

name: S. Joplin
bio: American composer and pianist who wrote carefully notated rags and waltzes as well as the opera Treemonisha. In 1976 he received a posthumous special Pulitzer award for his contribution to American music.

name: L. Godowsky
bio: Polish-American pianist and composer. His 53 Studies on Chopin's Etudes recompose the originals and are among the most demanding works in the piano repertoire.

name: Z. Stojowski
bio: Polish composer and pianist who studied with Paderewski and Delibes, and emigrated to the United States in 1905. He taught at the Institute of Musical Art in New York and wrote concertos for piano and violin as well as chamber music.

name: A. Scriabin
bio: Russian composer and pianist whose earliest piano pieces resemble Chopin's and who later developed a highly dissonant musical language that transcended traditional tonality. His ten piano sonatas trace a stylistic evolution from conventional late-Romantic beginnings to very different late works.

name: S. Rachmaninoff
bio: Russian composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor of the late Romantic era, known for sweeping lyricism.

name: J. Jongen
bio: Belgian composer and organist who taught at the Brussels Conservatoire and later directed it. His Symphonie concertante is for organ and orchestra, and his Aria et Polonaise for trombone was a Brussels Conservatoire competition piece in 1944.

name: C. Ives
bio: American composer and insurance executive whose experiments in polytonality and collage foreshadowed many musical innovations of the twentieth century. His Concord Sonata is a series of meditations on four Transcendentalist writers.

name: J. Lhévinne
bio: Russian-American pianist whose performances of the concertos of Chopin and Tchaikovsky were particularly notable. He and his wife Rosina Lhévinne gave duo-piano concerts together as partners, and both taught at the Juilliard School.

name: M. Ravel
bio: French composer known for his meticulous craftsmanship and dazzling orchestration. His piano works include Gaspard de la nuit, Jeux d'eau, and the Piano Concerto in G.

name: J. Hofmann
bio: Polish-American virtuoso regarded as one of the greatest pianists of the early twentieth century and the only private pupil of Anton Rubinstein. A child prodigy, he later directed the Curtis Institute of Music, and Rachmaninoff dedicated his Third Piano Concerto to him.

name: M. de Falla
bio: Spanish composer and pianist, one of Spain's most important musicians of the first half of the 20th century. His music shows the influence of the folk music of Andalusia and of Debussy and Ravel, whom he met in Paris; his works include the ballet El amor brujo, Nights in the Gardens of Spain for piano and orchestra, and the solo piano piece Fantasía bætica.

name: I. Vengerova
bio: Russian-American pianist and pedagogue who studied with Leschetizky and helped found the Curtis Institute of Music in 1924. A demanding teacher, her pupils included Gary Graffman, Samuel Barber, and Leonard Bernstein.

name: A. Cortot
bio: Swiss pianist, conductor, and teacher who lived and worked in France, counted among the foremost musicians of the twentieth century. He was especially valued for his poetic insight into Romantic piano works, particularly those of Chopin and Schumann, formed a trio with violinist Jacques Thibaud and cellist Pablo Casals, and co-founded the Ecole Normale de Musique de Paris.

name: E. Dohnányi
bio: Hungarian pianist, composer, and conductor. His Variations on a Nursery Tune for piano and orchestra parodies many composers of his day, while Ruralia Hungarica draws on Hungarian folk material.

name: S. Bortkiewicz
bio: Ukrainian-born composer and pianist who settled in Vienna after the Russian Revolution. He wrote piano concertos.

name: N. Medtner
bio: Russian pianist and composer who wrote almost exclusively for piano or with piano accompaniment. His Fairy Tales, sonatas, and three piano concertos represent a continuation of the Romantic tradition.

name: R. Lhévinne
bio: Russian-American pianist who taught at the Juilliard School for over 50 years. A gold medalist of the Moscow Conservatory, her students included Van Cliburn, John Browning, and Garrick Ohlsson.

name: E. Bloch
bio: Swiss-born American composer of Jewish descent, several of whose most notable works reflect his Jewish heritage. Best known for Schelomo for cello and orchestra, he also wrote a violin concerto, a piano quintet and the Symphony for Trombone and Orchestra.

name: G. Enescu
bio: Romanian composer, violinist, and conductor widely regarded as his country's most important musician. His Romanian Rhapsodies drew on folk material, and he mentored violinists including Yehudi Menuhin.

name: B. Bartók
bio: Hungarian composer, pianist, and ethnomusicologist whose work is often described as a combination of traditional peasant folk music and avant-garde music. He wrote three piano concertos, and his writing for the piano is often percussive.

name: V. Blazhevich
bio: Russian trombonist, composer and teacher who was principal trombone of the Bolshoi Theatre orchestra until 1928 and a professor at the Moscow Conservatory. He wrote many trombone concertos, etudes and method books, including the School for Trombone in Clefs.

name: A. Jørgensen
bio: Danish composer and violist, solo violist of the Royal Danish Orchestra from 1932, who wrote chiefly for brass as well as orchestral, chamber and vocal music. His Romance, Op. 21, and Suite, Op. 22, are for trombone.

name: K. Szymanowski
bio: Polish composer widely regarded as the country's most significant since Chopin, whose impressionist-influenced piano works include the Métopes and Masques suites. He served as director of the Warsaw Conservatory and undertook to create a Polish national style.

name: I. Stravinsky
bio: Russian-born composer who revolutionized music with The Rite of Spring. His piano works include Three Movements from Petrushka, the Concerto for Piano and Wind Instruments, and Movements for Piano and Orchestra.

name: A. Schnabel
bio: Austrian pianist and composer who studied with Leschetizky and made the first complete recording of Beethoven's piano sonatas (1932-35). He was known for his intellectual approach to the Austro-German repertoire.

name: P. Grainger
bio: Australian-born composer and pianist who later settled in the United States, known for settings such as Country Gardens and Molly on the Shore. His biographer John Bird considered Lincolnshire Posy his masterpiece; he also championed Grieg's music and developed machines to realise his ideas of 'free music'.

name: R.N. Dett
bio: Canadian-born American composer, pianist, and choral conductor who wove African-American spirituals into concert forms. His piano suite In the Bottoms includes the "Juba Dance."

name: I. Friedman
bio: Polish pianist and composer celebrated for his Chopin mazurkas. He gave thousands of concerts and edited Chopin's works for Breitkopf & Härtel.

name: A. Casella
bio: Italian composer, pianist, and conductor. His piano output ranges from the early solo Toccata, Op. 6 to later works such as the Nove pezzi and Sei studi, alongside Scarlattiana for piano and small orchestra.

name: W. Backhaus
bio: German pianist and pupil of Eugen d'Albert who won the Anton Rubinstein Competition in 1905 and, in 1928, became the first pianist to record Chopin's complete Études. He recorded the complete Beethoven piano sonatas in the 1950s and '60s, and was controversial for his support of the Nazi regime in the 1930s.

name: Y. Bowen
bio: English composer and pianist who studied at the Royal Academy of Music under Tobias Matthay and later taught there. Sometimes dubbed the 'English Rachmaninoff', he wrote four piano concertos.

name: D. Pejačević
bio: Croatian composer and pianist. She wrote the first Croatian piano concerto (1913), a Symphony in F-sharp minor regarded as the first modern Croatian symphony, and two violin sonatas.

name: J. Achron
bio: Russian-born violinist and composer who studied with Leopold Auer and became a leading figure of the Jewish national school. He settled in the United States in 1925 and is best remembered for his Hebrew Melody for violin and piano.

name: A. Rubinstein
bio: Polish-American pianist widely regarded as one of the greatest of the 20th century, especially celebrated for his interpretations of Chopin.

name: H. Villa-Lobos
bio: Brazilian composer who fused European classical forms with Brazilian folk and popular music. His piano output includes the cycle Prole do Bebê and the Rudepoêma, dedicated to Arthur Rubinstein.

name: F. Price
bio: American composer who in 1933 became the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra, when the Chicago Symphony premiered her Symphony No. 1 in E minor. Her music, including the Piano Sonata in E minor, combines African-American spirituals and dance idioms with classical forms.

name: H. Neuhaus
bio: Russian-Soviet pianist who taught at the Moscow Conservatory. His students included Sviatoslav Richter and Emil Gilels, and his book The Art of Piano Playing remains a standard text.

name: M. Hess
bio: English pianist best remembered for organizing the morale-boosting National Gallery concerts in London throughout World War II. She was celebrated for her performances of Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, and Schumann.

name: J. Ibert
bio: French composer whose elegant, witty style drew freely on Impressionism, neoclassicism, and jazz without ever belonging to a single school. His piano miniatures include the ten Histoires, and he also wrote the orchestral Escales and Divertissement.

name: B. Martinů
bio: Czech composer who settled in Paris and later the United States. His piano works include Esquisses and the Fantaisie et toccata.

name: F. Martin
bio: Swiss composer who developed a personal approach to twelve-tone technique. His output includes piano concertos and a violin concerto, and he wrote a Ballade for trombone and piano.

name: S. Prokofiev
bio: Russian composer and pianist whose nine piano sonatas and five piano concertos combine biting rhythmic energy, lyrical beauty, and sardonic wit. He was himself a formidable performer.

name: F. von Vecsey
bio: Hungarian violin prodigy who studied with Jenő Hubay in Budapest, played for Joseph Joachim in Berlin as a child and made his debut there at age ten. He toured Europe as a virtuoso, composed salon and virtuoso pieces for violin such as the Valse triste, and was the dedicatee of Sibelius's Violin Concerto.

name: C. Haskil
bio: Romanian pianist celebrated above all as one of the greatest interpreters of Mozart, prized for the clarity and unaffected naturalness of her playing. Frequent illness and extreme stage fright held back her career, and she began to win acclaim only after World War II; she toured and recorded with violinist Arthur Grumiaux.

name: W. Kempff
bio: German pianist and composer best known for his interpretations of Beethoven and Schubert. He held masterclasses at Positano.

name: W. Still
bio: American composer known as the "Dean of African American Composers," whose Afro-American Symphony (1931) was the first symphony by a Black composer performed by a major American orchestra. He was also the first African American to conduct a major U.S. symphony orchestra and to have an opera staged by a major American opera company.

name: E. Korngold
bio: Austrian-American composer and child prodigy. His Violin Concerto in D major, drawn from his own film themes, became a staple of the 20th-century repertoire.

name: H. Cowell
bio: American composer and pianist who played tone clusters with fists, palms, and forearms. He taught John Cage.

name: G. Gershwin
bio: American composer and pianist who bridged jazz and classical music. His Rhapsody in Blue, Piano Concerto in F, and three Preludes brought the rhythms and harmonies of jazz into the concert hall.

name: F. Poulenc
bio: French composer and pianist, member of Les Six. He wrote a two-piano concerto.

name: D. Ellington
bio: American pianist, composer and bandleader who led his orchestra for half a century. Standards such as Mood Indigo, Sophisticated Lady and Take the A Train sit beside suites like Black, Brown and Beige.

name: A. Copland
bio: American composer who created a distinctly American sound in classical music. His works include Piano Variations (1930), a Piano Sonata (1939-41) and a Piano Fantasy (1957).

name: J. Tizol
bio: Puerto Rican valve trombonist and composer who played in Duke Ellington's orchestra for many years. He wrote Caravan and Perdido, which became jazz standards.

name: V. Horowitz
bio: Ukrainian-born American pianist widely regarded as one of the greatest of all time. Renowned for his extraordinary virtuosity, tonal color, and electrifying performances of Chopin, Liszt, Scriabin, and Rachmaninoff.

name: C. Arrau
bio: Chilean-American pianist widely considered one of the greatest pianists of the twentieth century, known for intellectual and deeply reflective interpretations. A leading authority on Beethoven, he was also famous for his recordings of Schubert, Brahms and Debussy, and recorded much of the piano music of Schumann, Chopin and Liszt.

name: R. Serkin
bio: Bohemian-born Austrian-American pianist. He directed the Curtis Institute and co-founded the Marlboro Music Festival.

name: E. Hines
bio: American jazz pianist and bandleader known for his 'trumpet-style' piano playing, often using fast octaves. He recorded duets with Louis Armstrong in the late 1920s and led his own band at the Grand Terrace for over a decade.

name: D. Shostakovich
bio: Soviet composer and pianist who composed a set of 24 Preludes and Fugues and two piano concertos.

name: O. Messiaen
bio: French composer and organist whose piano works, including Vingt regards sur l'enfant-Jésus, drew on birdsong, Catholic theology and innovative rhythmic techniques. He was the teacher of Boulez and Stockhausen.

name: A. Tatum
bio: American jazz pianist whose blistering virtuosity, harmonic daring and rhythmic freedom influenced pianists such as Oscar Peterson and Bud Powell.

name: V. Holmboe
bio: Danish composer whose works of 1950 to 1970 are largely characterized by the metamorphosis of thematic and motivic fragments. He wrote thirteen symphonies, a large number of string quartets and a Sonata for trombone (1987).

name: S. Barber
bio: American composer, pianist, conductor, baritone, and music educator whose music embraced lyricism and emotional expression and adopted elements of modernism after 1940.

name: M.L. Williams
bio: American jazz pianist and composer who wrote for swing bands and mentored bebop pioneers. She composed the Zodiac Suite and sacred jazz works.

name: J. Cage
bio: American avant-garde composer who invented the prepared piano and wrote Sonatas and Interludes for it. His silent piece 4'33" (written for any instrument, premiered at the piano by David Tudor in 1952) is his most famous work, and all of his music from 1951 onward was composed using chance procedures; his influence on countless composers, artists and writers is notable.

name: M. Bonds
bio: American composer and pianist, known especially for her arrangements of African American spirituals and frequent collaborations with poet Langston Hughes. Her works include The Ballad of the Brown King and settings of Hughes's poetry for voice and piano.

name: B. Britten
bio: English composer, conductor, and pianist who was the soloist at the premiere of his own Piano Concerto (1938). He was also celebrated as an accompanist, above all in his recital partnership with the tenor Peter Pears.

name: S. Richter
bio: Soviet pianist widely considered one of the greatest pianists of the 20th century, celebrated for his vast repertoire spanning Bach to Prokofiev. He was praised for the depth of his interpretations and his virtuoso technique.

name: A. Ginastera
bio: Argentine composer whose piano works include the Danzas argentinas and three piano sonatas. One of the most important 20th-century composers of the Americas.

name: E. Gilels
bio: Soviet pianist who was one of the foremost pianists of the 20th century.

name: D. Lipatti
bio: Romanian pianist whose career was cut short by Hodgkin's disease at age 33. He studied with Alfred Cortot in Paris.

name: T. Monk
bio: American pianist and composer known for his angular melodies and as a pioneer of bebop. His 'Round Midnight is one of the most recorded jazz standards composed by a jazz musician.

name: A.B. Michelangeli
bio: Italian pianist whose perfectionism and extraordinary tonal control made him a legendary and enigmatic figure in 20th-century pianism. His students included Maurizio Pollini and Martha Argerich.

name: I. Xenakis
bio: Greek-French composer, architect and engineer who pioneered the use of mathematical models in music, including stochastic processes. His solo works include Evryali for piano and Mikka for violin.

name: G. Ligeti
bio: Hungarian-Austrian composer whose cycle of 18 Études for piano is among the most important piano works of the late 20th century. His music explores complex textures, polyrhythms, and micropolyphony.

name: A. de Larrocha
bio: Spanish pianist known especially for her playing of the works of Granados and Albéniz. She studied with Frank Marshall, himself a student of Granados.

name: B. Powell
bio: American jazz pianist and composer. His compositions, including Un Poco Loco, have become jazz standards.

name: P. Boulez
bio: French composer, conductor, and writer who was a central figure in post-war musical modernism. His Third Piano Sonata uses controlled chance, and Structures for two pianos is his key total-serialist work.

name: O. Peterson
bio: Canadian jazz pianist and composer admired for his dazzling technique, swing and speed, with a touch rooted in Art Tatum and Nat King Cole. His Canadiana Suite and Night Train, and his numerous trio recordings, are among his notable work.

name: J. Castérède
bio: French composer and pianist who studied at the Paris Conservatoire with Messiaen and Tony Aubin and was appointed professor of solfège there in 1960. His works include a Wind Quintet (1953) and a Fantaisie concertante (1960) for bass trombone or tuba and piano.

name: W. S. Hartley
bio: American composer and professor at SUNY Fredonia from 1969 to 1991 who wrote music for saxophone, low brass, and symphonic wind ensemble. His works include the Sonata Concertante for trombone and piano (1958).

name: K. Stockhausen
bio: German composer and pioneer of electronic and serial music. His Klavierstücke (Piano Pieces) push the boundaries of rhythm, dynamics, and keyboard technique.

name: L. Fleisher
bio: American pianist and conductor who studied with Artur Schnabel and overcame focal dystonia in his right hand. His students included André Watts and Hélène Grimaud.

name: G. Graffman
bio: American pianist and pedagogue who served as director and president of the Curtis Institute. He taught Lang Lang and Yuja Wang.

name: T. Takemitsu
bio: Japanese composer whose piano works include Rain Tree Sketch (1982) and Les yeux clos (1979).

name: F. Gulda
bio: Austrian pianist and composer known for his interpretations of the Viennese classics and boundary-crossing explorations of jazz. His students included Martha Argerich, who called him her most important influence.

name: A. Brendel
bio: Czech-born Austrian pianist, poet, and author, and the first pianist to record Beethoven's complete works for solo piano. He made three sets of the complete Beethoven sonatas, the first for Vox, and performed series of music by Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, and Liszt. His playing was sometimes described as cerebral.

name: G. Gould
bio: Canadian pianist renowned for his idiosyncratic interpretations of Bach, particularly the Goldberg Variations. His unconventional approach and early retreat from concerts to focus on recording are well known.

name: V. Cliburn
bio: American pianist who won the inaugural International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow in 1958, during the Cold War. He was a student of Rosina Lhévinne at Juilliard.

name: A. Schnittke
bio: Russian-German composer known for his 'polystylism.' His output includes symphonies, concerti grossi, and chamber music.

name: A. Pärt
bio: Estonian composer and the world's most performed living composer, known for his tintinnabuli technique. His piano work Für Alina is considered the first example of this meditative, bell-like style.

name: F. Rabe
bio: Swedish composer and trombonist who began as a jazz trombonist and later wrote electronic and choral music. His choral work Rondes (1964) is regarded as his most-performed piece, and he studied at the Royal College of Music in Stockholm and later worked as a producer at Swedish Radio.

name: S. Reich
bio: American composer and a pioneer of minimal music, using techniques such as phasing and repetitive patterns. His works include Piano Phase (1967) and Six Pianos (1973), and his style has influenced many contemporary composers.

name: P. Glass
bio: American composer and pianist who pioneered minimalism in classical music. His 20 piano études and numerous film scores have made him one of the most widely recognized living composers.

name: V. Ashkenazy
bio: Russian-Icelandic pianist and conductor who made recordings of Chopin (complete works for solo piano), Rachmaninoff, and the complete Beethoven piano sonatas. He retired from public performance in 2020.

name: N. Kapustin
bio: Ukrainian-Russian composer and pianist who uniquely fused jazz idioms with classical forms. His virtuosic concert études and sonatas are among his works.

name: V. Silvestrov
bio: Ukrainian composer who moved from Soviet avant-garde experiment to a later style. His Bagatelles and Kitsch-Music are works for piano.

name: F. Rzewski
bio: American composer-pianist whose works include the hour-long variations The People United Will Never Be Defeated! He premiered works from Stockhausen to his own.

name: M. Argerich
bio: Argentine pianist widely considered one of the greatest alive. She won the International Chopin Piano Competition in 1965.

name: M. Pollini
bio: Italian pianist who won the International Chopin Competition at age 18 and was known for his exceptional technique.

name: N. Freire
bio: Brazilian classical pianist whose recorded repertory is made up largely of Chopin, Schumann, Brahms, Beethoven, Debussy and Liszt. His longest piano-duo partnership was with Martha Argerich.

name: M. J. Pires
bio: Portuguese pianist, one of the leading interpreters of the 18th- and 19th-century repertoire, known for her interpretations of Mozart, Schubert, Chopin and Beethoven. She is Master in Residence at the Queen Elisabeth Music Chapel.

name: R. Lupu
bio: Romanian pianist acclaimed for his interpretations of Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, and Mozart. Famously reclusive, he often refused interviews and usually did not allow radio broadcasts of his performances; he made over 20 recordings for Decca from 1970 to 1993 and won an Edison Award and a Grammy.

name: A. Watts
bio: American pianist who, at age 16, performed with Leonard Bernstein on national television. A student of Leon Fleisher, he was one of the first Black classical soloists to achieve major international recognition.

name: J. Adams
bio: American composer and conductor whose music is usually categorized as minimalist or post-minimalist. His works include China Gates and Phrygian Gates for piano.

name: M. Perahia
bio: American pianist who was the first American to win the Leeds International Piano Competition (1972) and is renowned for his Bach and Mozart.

name: M. Uchida
bio: Japanese-British pianist. She recorded the complete Mozart piano sonatas and concertos.

name: E. Ax
bio: Polish-American pianist, born in Lviv, who won the inaugural Arthur Rubinstein International Piano Competition in 1974. He has won multiple Grammy Awards, several of them for chamber recordings with Yo-Yo Ma.

name: G. Sokolov
bio: Russian pianist who at age 16 became the youngest winner of the International Tchaikovsky Competition.

name: J. Hisaishi
bio: Japanese composer, conductor, and pianist, born Mamoru Fujisawa, best known for his scores for Hayao Miyazaki's Studio Ghibli films including My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away. He also scored several Takeshi Kitano films and tours widely performing his own music from the piano and the podium.

name: R. Sakamoto
bio: Japanese composer, pianist, and electronic music pioneer who shared the Academy Award for Best Original Score for The Last Emperor with David Byrne and Cong Su.

name: K. Saariaho
bio: Finnish composer celebrated for richly textured, spectral music exploring timbre and color, developed in part at IRCAM in Paris. Her opera L'Amour de loin, staged at the Metropolitan Opera in 2016, was the first opera by a woman there since 1903.

name: R. Anderson
bio: American jazz trombonist and composer known for extended techniques and wide-ranging bands, including the Slickaphonics and the Pocket Brass Band.

name: A. Schiff
bio: Hungarian-born British pianist and conductor renowned for his Bach, Haydn, Mozart, and Schubert. He founded the chamber orchestra Cappella Andrea Barca in 1999 and recorded the complete Beethoven sonatas live in concert.

name: J. de Meij
bio: Dutch composer, conductor and trombonist best known for his Symphony No. 1 'The Lord of the Rings', a work for wind band that won the 1989 Sudler Composition Award.

name: L. Einaudi
bio: Italian pianist and composer whose accessible style blends classical, pop, and minimalist elements. His albums have topped classical charts.

name: K. Zimerman
bio: Polish pianist who won the International Chopin Piano Competition in 1975 at age 18, its youngest-ever winner.

name: I. Pogorelich
bio: Croatian pianist whose controversial elimination from the 1980 Chopin Competition prompted Martha Argerich to resign from the jury in protest. His unorthodox interpretations continue to provoke debate.

name: Y. Bronfman
bio: Soviet-born American pianist. He studied with Rudolf Firkušný, Leon Fleisher, and Rudolf Serkin.

name: A. Hewitt
bio: Canadian pianist best known for her survey of Bach's keyboard works, recorded over more than a decade for Hyperion. She won the Toronto International Bach Piano Competition in 1985 and has toured her multi-recital Bach Odyssey worldwide.

name: M.-A. Hamelin
bio: Canadian virtuoso pianist and composer known for his phenomenal technique and active interest in little-known repertoire.

name: S. Hough
bio: British-Australian pianist, composer, and writer who was the first classical musician to receive a MacArthur Fellowship. His writings on music have appeared widely.

name: U. Chin
bio: South Korean composer based in Berlin and a pupil of Ligeti. She has six Piano Etudes.

name: F.P. Zimmermann
bio: German violinist whose repertoire includes music by Magnus Lindberg. He has recorded the complete Bach sonatas and partitas and plays the 1711 "Lady Inchiquin" Stradivari.

name: Max Richter
bio: German-born British composer and pianist whose work could be described as minimalist or postminimalist in style. His eight-and-a-half-hour concept album Sleep has been described as the most streamed classical record of all time.

name: H. Grimaud
bio: French pianist who is also a published author and wildlife advocate, and who founded the Wolf Conservation Center.

name: Y. Tiersen
bio: French composer and multi-instrumentalist who reached a worldwide audience through his score for the film Amélie (2001). Conservatory-trained on violin and piano in Rennes, Nantes, and Boulogne, he now writes and records from his own studio on the Breton island of Ushant.

name: E. Kissin
bio: Russian-born pianist who at age 12 performed Chopin's two piano concertos with the Moscow Philharmonic. He is especially known for his interpretations of Romantic-era music.

name: T. Adès
bio: British composer, pianist, and conductor who emerged as a leading figure in contemporary classical music. His operas include Powder Her Face, The Tempest, and The Exterminating Angel.

name: J. Montgomery
bio: American violinist and composer, a native of New York, whose works blend classical tradition with vernacular music and improvisation. Her string work Strum (2006, rev. 2012), available for string quartet, quintet or string orchestra, was named one of the 15 most significant string works of the 21st century by Strings magazine.

name: S. Blaser
bio: Swiss jazz trombonist and composer who has recorded widely for European labels.

name: Lang Lang
bio: Chinese concert pianist who has performed with leading orchestras worldwide.

name: N. Frahm
bio: German pianist and composer known for combining classical and electronic music. He has performed on a piano specially designed and made for him by David Klavins. His 2011 album Felt was met with critical acclaim, as was Spaces in 2013.

name: V. Ólafsson
bio: Icelandic pianist known for his interpretations of Bach, Rameau, and Philip Glass.

name: V. Frang
bio: Norwegian violinist whose repertoire includes Beethoven, Mendelssohn, Elgar, Korngold and Britten. She studied with Kolja Blacher, was mentored by Anne-Sophie Mutter, records for Warner Classics and has performed with orchestras including the Vienna Philharmonic and Philharmonia Orchestra.

name: Y. Wang
bio: Chinese-born pianist celebrated for her virtuosity and charismatic stage presence. She performs with leading orchestras worldwide and is a Grammy winner (Best Classical Instrumental Solo, 2024).

name: K. Buniatishvili
bio: Georgian pianist and Sony Classical recording artist. She has performed and recorded works by Liszt, Chopin, and Rachmaninoff.

name: I. Levit
bio: Russian-German pianist hailed as one of the most important artists of his generation. A Gilmore Artist Award recipient.

name: T. Hamasyan
bio: Armenian pianist and composer who fuses jazz improvisation with Armenian folk melody. He won the Thelonious Monk competition.

name: D. Trifonov
bio: Russian pianist and composer. He won the Tchaikovsky and Rubinstein competitions.

name: S.-J. Cho
bio: South Korean pianist who became the first from his country to win the International Chopin Piano Competition in 2015. He is an exclusive Deutsche Grammophon artist.

name: J. Lisiecki
bio: Canadian pianist of Polish heritage who signed with Deutsche Grammophon at age 15. Known for his poetic sensitivity.

name: T. Ono
bio: Japanese pianist and composer based in Germany who studied at TOHO Music College Tokyo before moving to Germany in 1999, completing her concert exam with distinction in Nuremberg. Her compositions include the piano and orchestra work 5 Elements and JIKU-Timeline Op.25, selected as a compulsory piece for the Friedrich Kuhlau International Flute Competition. She organizes the concert series Kunst trifft Komposition and performs in the duo Ensemble Lunata as pianist and composer.

name: H. Biber
bio: Bohemian-born composer and violinist active mainly in Salzburg. His violin music makes use of high positions and scordatura tunings, notably in his Mystery Sonatas.

name: A. Corelli
bio: Italian violinist and composer who helped place the violin among the most prestigious solo instruments in the Baroque era. His works include twelve concerti grossi (Op. 6), which Handel took as models for his own Op. 6 concerti grossi, and sonatas for violin (Op. 5).

name: A. Vivaldi
bio: Italian Baroque composer and virtuoso violinist who wrote approximately 230 violin concertos, including The Four Seasons. He influenced J.S. Bach.

name: F. Geminiani
bio: Italian violinist and composer who studied with Corelli and became a violin virtuoso in London. His treatise The Art of Playing on the Violin (1751) is the best-known summation of the 18th-century Italian method of violin playing.

name: G. Tartini
bio: Italian Baroque violinist and composer best known for his Devil's Trill Sonata. He founded an influential violin school in Padua and is credited with the discovery of combination tones (Tartini tones) in acoustics.

name: P. Locatelli
bio: Italian Baroque violinist and composer who studied in Rome, probably with Montanari or Valentini and perhaps briefly with Corelli. His L'Arte del Violino (1733) pairs twelve concertos with 24 capriccios containing some of the most difficult violin display passages of all Baroque literature.

name: J.-M. Leclair
bio: French Baroque violinist and composer who is considered to have founded the French violin school. He was renowned as both a violinist and a composer, and is best known for his violin sonatas and concertos.

name: C. de Seixas
bio: Portuguese composer and organist, appointed to the royal chapel in Lisbon while still a teenager. Of his hundreds of credited keyboard sonatas, about a hundred survive.

name: J. Bologne
bio: French violinist, composer, and conductor, born in Guadeloupe to a French planter father and an enslaved African mother, among the first known classical composers of African descent. He conducted the Concert des Amateurs and led the Concert de la Loge Olympique in Paris, and wrote violin concertos and symphonies concertantes.

name: L. Koželuch
bio: Bohemian composer and pianist who succeeded Mozart as court composer in Vienna. His roughly fifty piano sonatas and twenty-two surviving keyboard concertos were widely published, and he arranged Scottish, Irish and Welsh folk songs for the publisher George Thomson.

name: G.B. Viotti
bio: Italian violinist and composer whose 29 violin concertos are among his best-known works.

name: R. Kreutzer
bio: French violinist and composer whose 42 Études ou Caprices remain an essential part of violin pedagogy. Beethoven dedicated his Violin Sonata No. 9, the famous "Kreutzer Sonata," to him.

name: P. Baillot
bio: French violinist and pedagogue who studied with Viotti. He wrote the treatise L'Art du violon (1834).

name: P. Rode
bio: French violinist and composer who was a favourite pupil of Viotti. His 24 Caprices for solo violin remain widely used in violin education.

name: N. Paganini
bio: Italian violinist and composer, the most celebrated violin virtuoso of his time and one of the pillars of modern violin technique. His 24 Caprices for solo violin are among his best-known works and inspired pieces by Liszt, Schumann, Brahms and Rachmaninoff.

name: L. Spohr
bio: German violinist, composer, and conductor. He composed eighteen violin concertos and invented the violin chin rest around 1820.

name: F. Ries
bio: German pianist and composer, Beethoven's pupil, copyist, and later his biographer. He toured Europe before becoming a director of the Lower Rhine Music Festival.

name: A. Bazzini
bio: Italian violinist and composer, regarded as one of the finest concert violinists of the nineteenth century. His chamber music is his most enduring work and earned him a central place in Italy's instrumental renaissance. His compositions include six string quartets and several concertos, and he became director of the Milan Conservatory in 1882.

name: H. Vieuxtemps
bio: Belgian violinist and composer who was one of the most important figures in the Franco-Belgian violin school. His seven violin concertos, especially Nos. 4 and 5, remain staples of the Romantic violin repertoire.

name: J. Joachim
bio: Hungarian-born German violinist and composer. He was a close collaborator of Brahms, who wrote his Violin Concerto for Joachim.

name: H. Wieniawski
bio: Polish violinist and composer considered one of the greatest violin virtuosos of the 19th century. He wrote two violin concertos and works such as the Polonaise brillante, Op. 21.

name: P. de Sarasate
bio: Spanish violin virtuoso and composer, one of the most famous violinists of his day, admired for the purity of his tone and the effortless ease of his technique. His showpieces include Zigeunerweisen and the Carmen Fantasy.

name: L. Auer
bio: Hungarian-born violinist whose students at the St. Petersburg Conservatory included Heifetz, Milstein, and Elman. Tchaikovsky originally dedicated his Violin Concerto to him.

name: A. Backer Grøndahl
bio: Norwegian pianist and composer, a celebrated interpreter of Grieg's piano concerto who toured widely in Scandinavia and Britain. She studied with Hans von Bülow, drew high praise from George Bernard Shaw in 1889-90, and was a prominent figure in Norwegian musical life; her compositions include concert etudes, piano pieces and songs.

name: E. Ysaÿe
bio: Belgian violinist, conductor, and composer. He composed his Six Sonatas for Solo Violin, Op. 27, in 1923-1924, dedicating each to a different violinist.

name: M. Bonis
bio: French composer and pianist, a classmate of Debussy at the Paris Conservatoire, who published under the androgynous name 'Mel Bonis' to escape prejudice. Her three hundred works include many for piano.

name: S. Lyapunov
bio: Russian composer and pianist, the most important member of Balakirev's later circle. His twelve Transcendental Etudes completed the cycle of the 24 major and minor keys that Liszt had started.

name: M. Powell
bio: American violinist who gained international acclaim for her skill and virtuosity, the first American violinist to achieve international rank. She was among the first instrumentalists to make Red Seal records for the Victor Talking Machine Company and was soloist in the first American performances of the Tchaikovsky and Sibelius violin concertos.

name: F. Kreisler
bio: Austrian-born American violinist and composer known for his warm tone. His short character pieces and cadenzas for the Beethoven and Brahms concertos remain staples of the violin repertoire.

name: A. Berg
bio: Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School who combined Romantic lyricism with twelve-tone technique. Best known for the operas Wozzeck and Lulu, he also wrote an elegiac Violin Concerto.

name: M. Elman
bio: Russian-American violinist and pupil of Leopold Auer, whose sound became known simply as the "Elman tone." A child prodigy, he made his Berlin debut at thirteen.

name: J. Heifetz
bio: Lithuanian-born American violinist widely regarded as one of the greatest violinists of all time. A pupil of Leopold Auer, his dazzling virtuosity and intense tone set standards that strongly influenced how modern violinists approach the instrument.

name: E. Morini
bio: Austrian-American violinist and pupil of Otakar Ševčík at the Vienna Conservatory, who made her debut with the Berlin Philharmonic under Arthur Nikisch. She enjoyed a major international career spanning six decades, performing on a celebrated 1727 Stradivarius that was stolen from her New York apartment shortly before her death.

name: N. Milstein
bio: Ukrainian-born American violinist who studied first with Pyotr Stolyarsky in Odessa, then with Leopold Auer, and worked informally with Eugène Ysaÿe. Known for his impeccable technique and burnished tone, his interpretations of the Bach solo sonatas and partitas are regarded as definitive.

name: A. Khachaturian
bio: Armenian composer who wrote the ballet Gayane, which contains the Sabre Dance.

name: D. Oistrakh
bio: Soviet violinist considered one of the greatest of the 20th century, renowned for his warm tone and commanding technique. He was the dedicatee of both Shostakovich violin concertos and Prokofiev's Violin Sonata No. 1.

name: Y. Menuhin
bio: American-born British violinist and conductor who was one of the greatest child prodigies in music history. He later became a tireless humanitarian and advocate for music education, founding the Yehudi Menuhin School in 1962.

name: R. Ricci
bio: American violinist and child prodigy, known for his performances and recordings of the works of Paganini, whose 24 Caprices he was the first violinist to record in their original form (1947). He performed the world premieres of pieces by many contemporary composers, and his discography includes more than 500 recordings.

name: H. Szeryng
bio: Polish-born Mexican violinist. He served as a Mexican cultural ambassador and spoke seven languages fluently.

name: I. Stern
bio: Ukrainian-born American violinist. He saved Carnegie Hall from demolition, helped finance the studies of Perlman and Zukerman, and was a mentor to Shlomo Mintz.

name: A. Grumiaux
bio: Belgian violinist renowned for the beauty of his tone.

name: L. Kogan
bio: Soviet violinist who won the Queen Elisabeth Competition in 1951 and was one of the leading violinists of his generation.

name: I. Haendel
bio: Polish-born British violinist who was a child prodigy. She recorded the Sibelius, Elgar, and Brahms concertos.

name: C. Ferras
bio: French violinist who formed a celebrated recital partnership with pianist Pierre Barbizet.

name: I. Perlman
bio: Israeli-American violinist who contracted polio at age four and has walked using leg braces and crutches since then.

name: G. Kremer
bio: Latvian violinist who studied with David Oistrakh at the Moscow Conservatory and founded the Kremerata Baltica chamber orchestra.

name: K. Chung
bio: Korean violinist who shared first prize at the 1967 Leventritt Competition. Her recordings include the Tchaikovsky and Sibelius concertos.

name: V. Mullova
bio: Russian-born violinist who won the 1980 Sibelius Competition and the 1982 Tchaikovsky Competition before defecting to the West in 1983. She has also recorded world, jazz and pop music.

name: P. Zukerman
bio: Israeli-American violinist, violist, and conductor.

name: A.-S. Mutter
bio: German violinist who was discovered by Herbert von Karajan at age thirteen. She has premiered works by Lutoslawski, Dutilleux, Penderecki, and Previn.

name: J. Bell
bio: American violinist who made his Carnegie Hall debut at age seventeen. He gained wider fame through his incognito performance in a Washington, D.C. Metro station as part of a social experiment.

name: L. Kavakos
bio: Greek violinist and conductor who won the Sibelius Competition in 1985 and the Paganini Competition in 1988. He has built a career as a soloist, chamber musician, and conductor.

name: C. Tetzlaff
bio: German violinist. He leads his own Tetzlaff Quartet and is a noted advocate for solo and chamber works alongside the standard concerto repertoire.

name: G. Shaham
bio: American violinist known for his flawless technique, and a Grammy Award winner.

name: V. Repin
bio: Russian violinist who, at age 17, became the youngest-ever winner of the violin section of the Queen Elisabeth Competition in Brussels. He is also active as a chamber musician.

name: Midori
bio: Japanese-American violinist celebrated as a child prodigy, making her debut with the New York Philharmonic at age eleven. A dedicated educator and United Nations Messenger of Peace, she has combined a distinguished solo career with extensive humanitarian and teaching work.

name: A. Meyers
bio: American violinist whose wide discography spans Bach to newly commissioned works, including concertos and solo pieces written for her by Mason Bates, John Corigliano, and Jakub Ciupiński. She performs on the 1741 "Vieuxtemps" Guarneri del Gesù, lent to her for life.

name: D. Hope
bio: South African-born violinist of Irish and German heritage who has been an exclusive Deutsche Grammophon artist since 2007. He has built a wide-ranging career as concerto soloist and chamber musician, and serves as music director of the Zurich Chamber Orchestra and the New Century Chamber Orchestra and as artistic director of the Frauenkirche Dresden.

name: R. Barton Pine
bio: American violinist who debuted with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra at age ten and became the first American and youngest-ever gold medalist at the International J.S. Bach Competition. She maintains an active performing career while championing works by Black composers through her own foundation.

name: M. Vengerov
bio: Russian-Israeli violinist and conductor who was a child prodigy, winning international competitions from age ten. He is also an active pedagogue.

name: R. Capuçon
bio: French violinist with a broad repertoire ranging from Baroque to contemporary music. He performs on the 1737 Guarneri del Gesù "Panette" once owned by Isaac Stern and directs several festivals, including the Aix-en-Provence Easter Festival.

name: J. Jansen
bio: Dutch violinist and chamber musician, recording for Decca Classics.

name: H. Hahn
bio: American violinist and noted champion of new works.

name: S. Chang
bio: American violinist who debuted with the New York Philharmonic and Philadelphia Orchestra at age eight. She released her first album on EMI Classics at age eleven and studied at the Juilliard School under Dorothy DeLay.

name: J. Fischer
bio: German violinist who won the Yehudi Menuhin Competition at the age of eleven and has since built a leading international career. She performed a Saint-Saens violin concerto and the Grieg piano concerto in a single 2008 concert.

name: R. Chen
bio: Taiwanese-Australian violinist who won the Queen Elisabeth Competition in 2009, where he was the youngest participant, after winning first prize in the senior division of the Yehudi Menuhin International Competition in 2008. Known as one of the first classical musicians of his stature to embrace social media.

name: J. Ehnes
bio: Canadian-American violinist and multiple Grammy and Juno Award winner who performs on the 1715 "ex-Marsick" Stradivarius and leads the Ehnes Quartet.

name: L. Josefowicz
bio: Canadian-born American violinist devoted to contemporary music, with major concertos written for her by John Adams, Esa-Pekka Salonen, and Steven Mackey. She received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2008 in recognition of that advocacy.

name: A. Hadelich
bio: German-American violinist, born in Italy, who won the gold medal at the 2006 International Violin Competition of Indianapolis. Known for his expansive repertoire, he won a 2016 Grammy Award for his recording of Dutilleux's L'arbre des songes with the Seattle Symphony and is a noted champion of contemporary music.

name: N. Benedetti
bio: Scottish violinist who won BBC Young Musician of the Year at sixteen. In 2022 she became the first woman to serve as Director of the Edinburgh International Festival.

name: G. Gabrieli
bio: Italian composer and organist at St. Mark's Basilica in Venice, known for polychoral works for voices and instruments, including brass ensembles with sackbuts. His Sonata pian' e forte (1597) is one of the earliest pieces to specify dynamics and instrumentation.

name: C. Monteverdi
bio: Italian composer who bridged the Renaissance and Baroque eras. His opera L'Orfeo (1607) calls for four or five sackbuts within a brass group associated mainly with the Underworld scenes.

name: T. Tomkins
bio: Welsh-born composer and organist who almost certainly studied with Byrd and who served Worcester Cathedral and the Chapel Royal. His keyboard variations, preserved in a manuscript he copied in his final years, belong to the English virginal school.

name: H. Schütz
bio: German early Baroque composer regarded as the most important German composer before J.S. Bach. A pupil of Giovanni Gabrieli in Venice, his sacred concerto Fili mi, Absalon (SWV 269, Symphoniae sacrae I, 1629) is scored for solo bass, trombones and continuo.

name: S. Scheidt
bio: German organist and composer whose Tabulatura Nova (1624), a landmark collection of keyboard music, was notated in score on staves rather than letter tablature. A pupil of Sweelinck, he served as court organist and later Kapellmeister to the Margrave of Brandenburg in Halle, then as musical director of three churches there from 1628.

name: D. Speer
bio: German Baroque composer and writer who wrote sonatas for trombones and cornetts with basso continuo. He published a music treatise in 1687 that was influential on German Baroque trombone works.

name: J.C. Pezel
bio: German Baroque composer and Stadtpfeifer (town musician) in Leipzig and Bautzen, best known for his brass ensemble music for cornetts and trombones, including the Hora decima sonatas and Turmmusik written for tower musicians.

name: G.C. Wagenseil
bio: Austrian composer and pupil of J.J. Fux who served at the Vienna court. His Concerto for Alto Trombone (c. 1763) is among the earliest concerto-form solo works for the instrument.

name: L. Mozart
bio: German composer, violinist, and music theorist, best known as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's father and teacher. His Serenade (1755) contains alto trombone movements that are published as standalone concertos.

name: J.G. Albrechtsberger
bio: Austrian composer, organist, and music theorist who became Kapellmeister of St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna.

name: M. Haydn
bio: Austrian Classical-era composer who served as concertmaster in Salzburg and was the younger brother of Joseph Haydn. He wrote multiple works featuring trombone, including a Concerto in D major for alto trombone.

name: J.B. Vanhal
bio: Bohemian-born composer and teacher who reportedly played quartets with Haydn and Mozart. A prolific composer, he is credited with at least 73 symphonies and about 100 string quartets, and his piano music, written for a growing middle class, let him live a modest, economically independent life.

name: M. Martines
bio: Austrian composer, singer, and pianist. A pupil of Haydn and friend of Mozart, she wrote keyboard concertos and sonatas, and her name and music were known throughout Europe.

name: F.A. Belcke
bio: German trombonist who is probably the first trombone soloist ever heard in a German concert hall, at the Leipzig Gewandhaus in 1815. He served in the Berlin royal chapel from 1816 to 1858, toured Denmark, Sweden, Holland, France and Austria, and composed concertos, a duo and studies for trombone.

name: C.T. Queisser
bio: German trombonist and violist, known throughout Germany as a trombone soloist. He played trombone and viola in the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra under Mendelssohn, serving as principal viola in the orchestra and its quartet; Schumann called him a 'Posaunengott', and Ferdinand David's Concertino was dedicated to him.

name: A. Dieppo
bio: Dutch-born French trombonist who served as professor of trombone at the Conservatoire de Paris from 1836 to 1871 and authored one of the first reference methods for the instrument. He was much appreciated by Berlioz, who wrote the trombone solo of the Oraison funèbre in the Symphonie funèbre et triomphale notably for him.

name: F. David
bio: German violinist, composer, and conductor who served as concertmaster at the Leipzig Gewandhaus under Mendelssohn. His Concertino for Trombone and Orchestra, Op. 4, written for Karl Traugott Queisser, became the most popular 19th-century solo trombone work.

name: A. Guilmant
bio: French organist and composer, one of the leading concert organists of his era and a co-founder of the Paris Schola Cantorum. His eight organ sonatas were conceived for the Cavaillé-Coll organ of La Trinité, and his Morceau symphonique, Op. 88 (1902), for trombone and piano has become a cornerstone of the trombone repertoire.

name: Rimsky-Korsakov
bio: Russian composer and member of The Five, best known for orchestral works like Scheherazade. His Concerto for Trombone and Military Band was written in 1877.

name: A. Pryor
bio: American trombone virtuoso who joined the Sousa Band in 1892 and estimated he played 10,000 solos over 12 years. German Army band trombonists, amazed by his playing, reportedly insisted on taking his trombone apart, refusing to believe that it was natural.

name: L. Grøndahl
bio: Danish conductor and composer. He wrote a Trombone Concerto (1924).

name: Kid Ory
bio: Louisiana-born trombonist and composer whose tailgate style became central to the New Orleans trombone sound. He led one of the best-known bands in New Orleans in the 1910s, recorded with Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, and wrote the jazz standard Muskrat Ramble.

name: D. Milhaud
bio: French composer and member of Les Six, one of the most prolific composers of the 20th century, whose opus list ended at 443 and spanned a wide range of genres. His music makes extensive use of polytonality and is influenced by jazz and Brazilian music.

name: F. Mompou
bio: Catalan composer and pianist whose works include Música callada and Cançons i danses, the latter mostly based on existing Catalan folk tunes. He cultivated an aesthetic of silence and concentrated expression.

name: L. Boulanger
bio: French composer who in 1913 became the first woman to win the Prix de Rome, with the cantata Faust et Hélène. Chronically ill from childhood, she died at 24; her older sister was the composer and composition teacher Nadia Boulanger.

name: E. Schulhoff
bio: Czech composer and pianist who fused jazz, Dada, and neoclassicism during the interwar years. He wrote piano etudes, sonatas, and jazz-inspired suites; the Nazis suppressed his music, and he died of tuberculosis in 1942 in the Wülzburg internment camp in Bavaria.

name: P. Hindemith
bio: German-American composer, music theorist, and violist who was a major advocate of Neue Sachlichkeit. His Sonata for Trombone and Piano (1941) is a staple of the trombone repertoire.

name: G. Jacob
bio: English composer and teacher whose Trombone Concerto is one of the true standards of the original trombone solo literature. He was a professor of composition and orchestration at the Royal College of Music from 1924 until his retirement in 1966.

name: Miff Mole
bio: American trombonist credited with creating the first distinctive and influential solo jazz trombone style, featuring octave leaps, shakes and rapid-fire cadenzas. He recorded with Red Nichols and the Original Memphis Five, later worked at NBC, and influenced 1920s trombonists including Tommy Dorsey and Glenn Miller.

name: E. Lecuona
bio: Cuban composer and pianist, many of whose works, including Malagueña and Andalucía, have become standards of the Latin, jazz and classical repertoires.

name: H. Tomasi
bio: French composer and conductor of Corsican descent who studied at the Conservatoire de Paris. He composed his Concerto for Trombone in 1956.

name: G. Miller
bio: American big band leader, arranger, composer, and trombonist who wrote "Moonlight Serenade" and led the best-selling recording band from 1939 to 1942. He joined the U.S. Army Air Forces during WWII and was lost over the English Channel in 1944 when his plane disappeared.

name: J. Teagarden
bio: Largely self-taught Texas-born trombonist who developed unusual alternative positions and special effects on the trombone. He influenced later trombonists, and Tommy Dorsey said Teagarden heavily influenced his own playing style.

name: T. Dorsey
bio: Trombonist and bandleader known as the Sentimental Gentleman of Swing for his smooth-toned trombone playing. He led an extremely successful band from the late 1930s into the 1950s, amassing 286 Billboard chart hits.

name: E. Bozza
bio: French composer and conductor who won the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in 1934 and became one of the most prolific creators of chamber music for wind instruments in the 20th century. His works include the Ballade for trombone and piano (1944).

name: P. Creston
bio: Self-taught American composer of Sicilian immigrant parentage whose work tends to be fairly conservative in style, with a strong rhythmic element. His works include Fantasy for Trombone and Orchestra, Op. 42 (1947).

name: V. Dickenson
bio: American jazz trombonist whose career ran from the 1920s into the 1980s, known for the wit and vocalized phrasing of his swing and traditional-jazz playing. He recorded with Count Basie, recorded and toured with Sidney Bechet, and led the acclaimed Vic Dickenson Septet sessions for Vanguard.

name: L.-E. Larsson
bio: Swedish composer and conductor whose eclectic style ranged from late Romanticism to the twelve-note techniques he was the first Swede to employ. His Concertino for trombone and string orchestra is one of a series of twelve concertinos for solo instruments.

name: G. Bacewicz
bio: Polish composer and violinist who wrote piano sonatas and concert etudes.

name: J. Koetsier
